lessons.title: Commodities in a Portfolio — Correlation, Taxation, and Access

children.text: Every lesson so far has assumed you have a reason to be in a commodity market: a business exposure to hedge, or a directional or spread view to speculate on. But you may simply be an investor asking a calmer question: does gold, silver or a broader commodity allocation belong in a long-term portfolio at all? The nearly 46% jump in gold prices between April-May 2025 and April-May 2026, covered in Chapter 3, is exactly the kind of move that reopens that question for a lot of Indian investors. This closing lesson answers it across three angles: whether commodities genuinely diversify a portfolio, how they are actually taxed, and which vehicle, futures, ETFs, or a now-discontinued government bond, is the right way to hold them.

body.text: Commodities, especially gold, can diversify a portfolio because they respond to different forces than equities and bonds do. But the case for holding them depends just as much on how they are taxed and which access route you choose as it does on their price behaviour.

children.text: Equities are ultimately a claim on future corporate earnings. Gold is not, which is precisely why it tends to behave differently when the things that hurt corporate earnings, recession fear, currency weakness, geopolitical shocks, show up.

body.caption: How different stress scenarios typically play out for equities vs gold

cells: Sharp equity market sell-off / recession fear
Falls, often sharply
Often rises as investors seek a safe haven, though it can fall alongside everything else in the very first, most panicked days of a crisis
Rising inflation
Mixed to negative, especially for companies unable to pass on costs
Often rises, historically viewed as a store of value against currency debasement
Rupee depreciation
Mixed; export-oriented sectors can benefit
Rises in rupee terms even if the dollar price of gold is unchanged, since gold is priced globally in dollars
Geopolitical shock
Generally negative
Often rises on safe-haven demand

body.text: No correlation pattern is a guarantee. Gold has, on occasion, fallen alongside equities during the most acute phase of a liquidity crisis, when investors sell whatever they can to raise cash. Diversification benefits show up reliably over time and across many episodes, not in every single week of every single crisis.

children.text: Taxation: Futures Are Business Income, Not Capital Gains

This is the single most important tax fact in this course: profits and losses from commodity futures and options are not capital gains at all, regardless of how long you hold a position. They are chargeable as profits and gains of business or profession under Section 26 (old Section 28) of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Whether that business income is treated as non-speculative or speculative depends entirely on how the trade was executed.

body.caption: Non-speculative vs speculative treatment of commodity derivative income

cells: Where it applies
Trades executed electronically on a recognised exchange like MCX or NCDEX, through a registered broker, with a proper contract note carrying client codes and PAN
Trades that do not meet these conditions, such as informal off-exchange dealing
Governing definition
Defined as an eligible transaction under Section 66(31) (old Section 43(5)) of the Income-tax Act, 2025
Falls under the general speculative transaction definition in the same Section 66(31) (old Section 43(5))
Loss set-off
Can be set off against most other business income, and carried forward under general business loss rules
Can only be set off against other speculative business profits, carried forward for a maximum of four assessment years under Section 113 (old Section 73)

body.text: Everything covered in this course, exchange-traded MCX and NCDEX futures and options through a registered broker, sits squarely in the eligible, non-speculative category. This matters in practice: a bad year of losses on this basis is a normal, flexible business loss, not a narrowly restricted speculative one.

children.text: Two more practical points follow from business-income treatment. First, if your commodity trading turnover (computed conventionally as the absolute sum of profits and losses across trades, not notional contract value) crosses ₹1 crore in a year, or ₹10 crore if your cash receipts and cash payments are each 5% or less of the total, a tax audit becomes mandatory under Section 63 (old Section 44AB) of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Most traders operating entirely through a broker's digital platform will fall into the higher, ₹10 crore threshold, since almost none of their turnover is in cash. Second, every trade also carries a Commodities Transaction Tax (CTT) under the Finance Act, 2013, separate from income tax entirely: broadly 0.01% of trade value on the sell side for non-agricultural futures, and 0.05% of the premium on the sell side for non-agricultural options that are not exercised. Most agricultural commodities, a category that includes several contracts covered in this course, are exempt from CTT specifically to keep hedging accessible for farmers and processors.
Access: Futures vs ETFs vs a Now-Discontinued Government Bond

For an investor without a hedging need, wanting simple, long-term commodity exposure, futures are often not even the most convenient tool available. It is worth knowing all three routes, and knowing that one of them is no longer open to new investors at all.

body.text: This is the natural endpoint of the whole course: futures are a precision tool built for hedgers managing real exposure and traders expressing a specific view, not the default vehicle for a buy-and-hold portfolio allocation. An HNI investor wanting steady, long-term commodity exposure alongside equities and bonds will usually find a Gold ETF, taxed as a plain long-term capital asset after 12 months, a simpler fit than actively managing futures positions, margin calls and rollovers.

body.title: Futures or ETF?
body.scenario: Two investors both want gold exposure. Investor A is a jewellery exporter (from Chapter 3) who needs to lock in a gold purchase cost for a confirmed order two months from now. Investor B is a retired professional who wants to allocate 8% of a long-term investment portfolio to gold, planning to hold it for years as a diversifier alongside equities and bonds.
body.prompt: Which vehicle, futures or a Gold ETF, fits each investor better, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Investor A needs futures. Their need is a specific, time-bound hedge tied to a confirmed business transaction, and only a futures contract lets them lock in today's price for a purchase happening in exactly two months. Investor B is better served by a Gold ETF. They have no specific transaction to hedge, no interest in managing margin, mark-to-market or rollovers, and would benefit from the ETF's flat 12.5% long-term capital gains rate after 12 months rather than having every gain taxed as business income at their slab rate under futures.

body.title: Commodities in a Portfolio: Core Terms

cards.definition: A commodity derivative trade executed electronically on a recognised exchange through a registered intermediary with a proper contract note, qualifying for non-speculative business income treatment under Section 66(31) (old Section 43(5)) of the Income-tax Act, 2025.
A transaction-level tax under the Finance Act, 2013, on non-agricultural commodity futures and options, separate from income tax; most agricultural commodities are exempt.

The turnover level (₹1 crore, or ₹10 crore if cash receipts and payments are each 5% or less of turnover) beyond which a business, including commodity trading, must have its accounts audited under Section 63 (old Section 44AB) of the Income-tax Act, 2025.
A government-issued gold-linked bond; no new tranches have been issued since February 2024, and existing holders continue under their original terms.

points: Commodities, particularly gold, can diversify a portfolio by responding differently than equities to recession fear, inflation and currency weakness, though this pattern is not guaranteed in every crisis.

Commodity futures and options profits are always business income, not capital gains, chargeable under Section 26 (old Section 28) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, taxed at slab rate regardless of holding period.

Exchange-traded, broker-executed commodity trades qualify as eligible, non-speculative transactions under Section 66(31) (old Section 43(5)), with more flexible loss set-off than speculative trades, which are restricted under Section 113 (old Section 73).

A tax audit becomes mandatory under Section 63 (old Section 44AB) once turnover crosses ₹1 crore, or ₹10 crore for traders whose transactions are almost entirely non-cash, which covers most broker-platform commodity traders.

For long-term, unleveraged portfolio exposure rather than hedging or active trading, a Gold ETF, taxed at a flat 12.5% LTCG rate after 12 months, is usually a simpler fit than futures. Sovereign Gold Bonds are no longer available to new investors as of this writing.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Tax laws, rates, thresholds and section numbers can change, and their application depends on individual facts. Consult a qualified chartered accountant and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment or tax decisions.
